title: Backdoor Channels Hidden in Latent Space: Extending Cryptographic Undetectability to Modern Neural Networks
claim: A hidden backdoor can be built in three steps by finding a latent direction, planting a spike along it, and triggering it.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, numbered steps with colored arrows between them
description: Three rounded panels read left to right, titled 1 'Find the key', 2 'Plant the spike' and 3 'Open the backdoor'. Panel 1 is gray. It shows a 2-D scatter of blue and red points split by a dark slanted boundary bar, with a large orange key labeled ν_bd pointing along the boundary normal. Panel 2 is light blue. A circular isotropic Gaussian with a grid and blue points is multiplied by L/σ and becomes a stretched ellipse with an orange spike axis. A small weight-matrix icon turns into a door icon. Panel 3 is gray. Blue points move across the boundary toward the red cluster along orange-dashed arrows. An image plus noise trigger, tagged with a key, pushes a point across the boundary. Orange and blue arrows link the panels.
abstract: Recent cryptographic results establish that neural networks can be backdoored such that no efficient algorithm can distinguish them from a clean model. These guarantees, however, have been confined to stylised architectures of limited practical relevance, leaving open whether comparable undetectability extends to modern, end-to-end trained networks. We construct such an attack mechanism for deep neural network architectures, closely aligned to the cryptographic notion of undetectability, by identifying backdoor channels as learned latent directions, and show that the question of undetectability reduces to a hypothesis test between two unknown distributions over model parameters, which we conjecture to be intractable in practice. The consequence of this reframing is significant: if exploitable channels within a network's latent space are statistically indistinguishable from naturally learned directions, an attacker need not introduce foreign structure but can instead exploit the geometry the network already possesses. Demonstrating the approach on ResNet and Vision Transformer architectures trained on standard image classification datasets, the attack achieves both consistently high success rates with negligible clean accuracy degradation, and resists a comprehensive suite of post-training defences, none of which neutralise the backdoor without rendering the model unusable. Our results establish that cryptographic backdoors need not be artefacts requiring exotic architectures or artificial constructions, but identifiable as latent properties inherent to the geometry of learned representations.
